text:
Recent work supports testing which history segments matter, but does not establish the exact proposed GRU4Rec probe. A 2026 perturbation-based attribution study reports greater importance for recent interactions in GRU4Rec and measurable score changes after removing influential events; its MovieLens-100K findings need verification on the four Amazon categories ([paper](https://www.jidmis.org/index.php/jidmis/article/view/2525)). Earlier work explicitly applies recency-based training-example sampling to GRU4Rec, providing precedent for investigating recency, though this differs from removing prefixes while preserving targets ([Recency Sampling, 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643)). The original implementation also distinguishes independent sessions from whole-user histories and emphasizes correct recurrent-state handling ([GRU4Rec documentation](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec)).

Practical synthesis: evaluate the same trained GRU4Rec on full histories, prefixes removed, and suffixes removed, keeping each validation target and candidate set identical. Compare equal-size removals; repack retained events with left padding and read the final nonpadding state. Report paired target-rank changes and HR@10 differences by original history length and timestamp-derived target gap, with user-level paired bootstrap intervals. Hidden-state cosine distance can supplement ranking changes but does not establish usefulness. Suffix removal also increases the gap between retained context and target, so interpret it as recent-context dependence rather than a clean isolation of forgetting. Consistent improvements after prefix removal would motivate stochastic prefix cropping during training with unchanged next-item supervision; this remains a hypothesis requiring validation, not an established result. Keep one trained checkpoint per category; perturbations serve diagnosis only.
